tips.title: Pressure is collisions with the walls
tips.body: Every *explain* question in this topic starts from the same sentence: pressure is the **total force from particles colliding with the walls**, divided by the area. Then say whether the collisions have become **more frequent**, **harder**, or both.

tips.title: Which quantity is being held fixed?
tips.body: **Volume fixed and heated**: the particles speed up, so collisions are more frequent **and** harder, and no equation is needed. **Temperature fixed and squeezed**: the speed is unchanged and only the **frequency** rises, so use $pV = \text{constant}$.

tips.title: The units only have to match
tips.body: $p_1V_1 = p_2V_2$ works in kPa and cm³ just as well as Pa and m³, because the units cancel between the two sides. Convert only when the **two pressures** are in different units, the **two volumes** are in different units, or the question asks for a particular unit in the answer.

tips.title: Did it move the right way?
tips.body: At constant temperature, for a fixed mass of gas, pressure and volume are **inversely** proportional. Squeeze it and the pressure must go **up**; let it expand and the pressure must come **down**. If your answer moved the other way you divided the wrong way round.

why.matters:
A gas is invisible and you cannot hold it, so it is tempting to treat it as nothing. The particle model says it is billions of tiny collisions a second, and that turns three vague words, pressure, temperature and volume, into one picture that predicts each from the others.

Squeeze a gas and it pushes back harder; heat it and it pushes back harder; and you can say by how much. That is the whole of a bicycle pump, a car tyre, a diver's lungs and a bag of crisps on an aeroplane.

examples.title: Why the crisp packet puffs up on the plane
examples.body:
The bag was sealed at the shop with air at about 101 kPa. An airliner's cabin is kept at about 75 kPa, the pressure a couple of thousand metres up a mountain. Same air, same temperature; only the push from outside has dropped.

With less pressure holding it in, $pV$ stays fixed, so the air spreads until its own pressure has fallen to match: 100 cm³ at the shop becomes $100 \times 101 \div 75$, about 135 cm³. The bag goes tight as a drum, and a bottle sealed in the air is crushed on the way down for the same reason in reverse.

props.caption: The same air, the same temperature: the pressure fell, so the volume rose to keep pV the same.

visual.alt: Two bars drawn to scale showing one hundred cubic centimetres of air sealed at the shop swelling to one hundred and thirty five in an aircraft cabin at seventy five kilopascals

examples.title: Why a diver breathes out all the way up
examples.body:
At 20 m the water adds $20 \times 1 000 \times 9.8$ Pa to the atmosphere's 101 kPa: about 297 kPa in total, nearly three times the pressure at the surface. A diver's tank delivers air at that pressure, so a lungful down there holds nearly three times the air of a lungful on the beach.

Come up holding your breath and $pV$ = constant does the rest: as the pressure falls to 101 kPa, 1 litre of air wants to become 2.9 litres, and lungs cannot stretch that far. So the first rule of diving is to breathe out on the way up, and the extra simply leaves.

props.caption: A lungful taken at twenty metres, if it were carried to the surface unbreathed.

visual.alt: Two bars drawn to scale showing one litre of air breathed at twenty metres depth expanding to nearly three litres at the surface as the pressure falls from two hundred and ninety seven kilopascals to one hundred and one

examples.title: Why tyre pressures are checked cold
examples.body:
The sticker inside a car door gives the tyre pressures and says to check them cold. Half an hour of driving warms the air in the tyre: the rubber flexes and the brakes get hot. The tyre's volume hardly changes, so this is heating at constant volume.

Warmer particles move faster. They reach the walls more often and hit them harder, so the total force on the inside of the tyre rises and the pressure with it. Measure then and you would read high, let air out, and drive off next morning under-inflated. The same chain is why a sealed can must never go on a fire.

boxes.body: Air at the temperature of the garage. The gauge reads what the sticker says.

boxes.title: After half an hour
boxes.body: Flexing rubber and hot brakes have warmed the air inside. Same volume, same particles.

boxes.title: What changed
boxes.body: Faster particles reach the wall more often and hit it harder, so the pressure is up.

boxes.title: So the sticker says cold
boxes.body: Set the pressure warm and it will be low again by morning.

steps.title: What a gas actually is
steps.body:
In a gas the particles are far apart and move **randomly** at high speed in all directions. They collide with each other and with the walls of the container.

Two consequences carry almost every question in this topic.

- **Pressure comes from collisions.** Each particle hitting a wall exerts a tiny force. The **pressure** is the total force from all those collisions, divided by the area. More collisions, or harder ones, means more pressure.
- **Temperature is related to the average kinetic energy.** Raising the temperature makes the particles move **faster on average**. It is the *average* that matters, because at any moment some are fast and some are slow.

Both statements are worth learning word for word, because *explain* questions in this topic are marked on exactly this language.

check.prompt: What causes the pressure of a gas on the walls of its container?
check.solution: Each collision with a wall exerts a small force. The **pressure** is the total force from all those collisions divided by the area of the wall.

steps.title: Heating a gas at constant volume
steps.body:
Keep the volume fixed and raise the temperature. What happens to the pressure, and **why**?

The chain has three links, and a full-mark answer says all three:

1. The particles gain **kinetic energy**, so they move **faster**.
2. They hit the walls **more often**, and each collision is **harder**, so each transfers more momentum.
3. The total force on the walls rises, and since the area is unchanged, the **pressure rises**.

Stopping at "the particles move faster" earns the first mark only. The examiner wants the collisions and then the pressure.

This part of the specification is **qualitative**: no equation is required for the constant-volume case.

steps.title: Squeezing a gas: pV = constant
steps.body:
Now hold the **temperature** constant and change the volume. Squeeze a gas into half the space and the particles hit the walls twice as often, so the pressure doubles.

$$p V = \text{constant}$$

The equation is **given on the equation sheet**. In practice you use it as $p_1 V_1 = p_2 V_2$: work out the constant from the first pair, then divide by the new value.

This is **Physics only**, and it holds only at **constant temperature** for a **fixed mass** of gas.

check.prompt: A gas at 200 kPa fills 500 cm³. It is compressed to 250 cm³ at the same temperature. What is the new pressure, in kPa?
check.solution: $pV = 200 \times 500 = 100\,000$, so $p_2 = \dfrac{100\,000}{250} = 400$ kPa. Halving the volume doubles the pressure.

steps.title: Why squeezing raises the pressure
steps.body:
The calculation is easy; the **explanation** is what separates answers.

When the volume falls at constant temperature:

- The particles have the **same average kinetic energy**, because the temperature has not changed. They are **not** moving faster.
- There is **less space**, so each particle reaches a wall **sooner**, and the collisions become **more frequent**.
- More collisions per second means more total force on the walls, so the **pressure rises**.

The trap is saying the particles speed up. They do not: at constant temperature their average speed is unchanged. Only the **rate** of collisions changes, not their force.

Compare that with heating at constant volume, where the collisions become both more frequent **and** harder.

rows: more, because less space to cross
props.title: Both raise the pressure, for different reasons

visuals.alt: A table contrasting squeezing a gas at constant temperature with heating it at constant volume, showing which changes and which does not

steps.title: Your turn: a syringe
steps.body:
A sealed syringe holds **60 cm³** of air at atmospheric pressure, about **101 kPa**. The plunger is pushed in until the air occupies **20 cm³**, slowly enough that the temperature does not change.

1. Work out the constant $pV$.
2. Find the new pressure.
3. Explain, in terms of particles, why the pressure has risen.
4. Say why pushing the plunger **quickly** would give a different answer.

The last part is the Higher tier idea in the next step, so attempt it after reading on if you need to.

props.title: The product is the same in both rows

visuals.alt: A blank table for the syringe calculation, with columns for the pressure, the volume and their product

check.prompt: A syringe holds 60 cm³ of air at 101 kPa. The plunger is pushed in slowly until the air occupies 20 cm³. What is the new pressure, in kPa?
check.solution: $pV = 101 \times 60 = 6,060$, so $p_2 = \dfrac{6,060}{20} = 303$ kPa. The volume was cut to a third, so the pressure trebles.

steps.title: Going deeper: doing work on a gas
steps.body:
This part is **Higher tier**, and it explains why the slow-and-quick distinction matters.

Pushing a plunger in **does work** on the gas: a force moves through a distance. That work **transfers energy to the gas**, raising its **internal energy**. For a gas, a rise in internal energy shows up as a rise in **temperature**.

So compressing a gas quickly makes it **hotter**, which is why a bicycle pump warms up near the valve.

That is also why $pV = \text{constant}$ carries the condition **at constant temperature**. Compress slowly and the gas has time to lose the energy to the surroundings, so the temperature stays roughly constant and the equation holds. Compress quickly and it does not: the temperature rises, and the pressure ends up **higher** than $pV = \text{constant}$ predicts.

A question mentioning *rapidly* or *suddenly* is testing exactly this, and expects you to say the equation no longer applies.

visuals.alt: A table comparing compressing a gas slowly and rapidly, showing what happens to the temperature and whether the equation applies

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Gas particles move **randomly** at high speed in all directions.
- **Pressure** is the total force from particles **colliding with the walls**, divided by the area.
- **Temperature** is related to the **average kinetic energy** of the molecules.
- **Heat at constant volume**: particles move faster, so collisions are **more frequent and harder**, and the pressure rises. No equation is needed.
- **Squeeze at constant temperature**: the average speed is **unchanged**, but there is less space, so collisions are **more frequent**. The pressure rises.
- $pV = \text{constant}$, given on the sheet. Use it as $p_1V_1 = p_2V_2$: find the constant, then divide by the new value.
- The units only have to **match** between the two states; cm³ throughout is fine.
- At constant temperature, pressure and volume are **inversely** proportional: quarter the volume, four times the pressure.
- **Higher tier**: doing **work** on a gas raises its **internal energy** and so its **temperature**, which is why a rapid compression breaks the constant-temperature condition.
- **What is Physics only**: the particle motion in the first two steps is in combined science as well, but $pV = \text{constant}$ and work done on a gas are **Physics only**, and work done on a gas is also **Higher tier**.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The calculation.** For a fixed mass at constant temperature, $pV$ is the same before and after.

$$pV = 101 \times 60 = 6060$$

$$p_2 = \dfrac{6060}{20} = \mathbf{303} \text{ kPa}$$

**The explanation.** The temperature has **not** changed, so the average kinetic energy and therefore the **average speed** of the particles are unchanged. They are not moving faster.

What has changed is the **space**. The particles are confined to a third of the volume, so each reaches a wall sooner and collisions become about **three times as frequent**. More collisions each second means a greater total force on the same area, so the pressure is three times greater.

questions.prompt: Explain why heating a gas in a sealed rigid container raises its pressure, and why compressing a gas at constant temperature also raises its pressure, making clear how the two explanations differ.
questions.solution: When a gas in a sealed rigid container is heated, the particles gain kinetic energy and so move faster on average. Because they are moving faster they reach the walls more often, and each collision transfers more momentum, so each is harder. The total force on the walls therefore increases, and since the container is rigid the area is unchanged, so the pressure rises. When a gas is compressed at constant temperature the reason is different. The temperature has not changed, so the average kinetic energy and the average speed of the particles are exactly as before, and the collisions are no harder than they were. What changes is the space available: the particles have a shorter distance to travel before reaching a wall, so collisions become more frequent. The total force rises for that reason alone, and the pressure rises. In short, heating changes both the frequency and the force of the collisions, while compressing changes only the frequency.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Heating at constant volume.** The particles gain **kinetic energy**, so they move **faster**. Because they move faster they reach the walls **more often**, and each collision transfers more momentum, so each is **harder**. The total force on the walls rises, and the container is rigid so the area is unchanged: the **pressure rises**.

**Compressing at constant temperature.** The reason is different. The temperature has not changed, so the average kinetic energy and the **average speed are exactly as before**, and the collisions are **no harder**. What changes is the **space**: the particles have a shorter distance to cross before hitting a wall, so collisions become **more frequent**. That alone raises the total force, and the pressure rises.

**The difference.** Heating changes **both** the frequency and the force of the collisions. Compressing changes **only** the frequency.

examTechnique.body:
Decide first which quantity is being held fixed. A rigid sealed container means constant volume, and the answer is a particle explanation with no equation. A slow squeeze means constant temperature, and $pV = \text{constant}$ applies.

For a calculation, find the product $pV$ from the pair you are given, write it down, then divide by the new value. Writing the constant on its own line makes the method visible and stops you dividing the wrong way round.

The units on the two sides only have to **match**. Working in kPa and cm³ throughout is perfectly valid and saves two conversions.

For an explanation, give the full chain: what happens to the speed, what happens to the collisions, and therefore what happens to the pressure. Stopping at *the particles move faster* earns one mark of three.

Watch for the word **rapidly**. A quick compression does work on the gas and heats it, so the constant-temperature condition fails and the equation no longer applies.
examinerErrors: Saying the particles speed up when a gas is compressed at constant temperature. They do not.
Dividing the wrong way round, so squeezing a gas appears to lower its pressure.
Converting one quantity but not the other, so the units no longer match.
Stopping an explanation at 'the particles move faster' without reaching the collisions or the pressure.
Using pV = constant for a rapid compression, where the temperature rises.
Saying the particles themselves expand or get bigger when heated.
Forgetting that pV = constant needs a fixed mass of gas.
Assuming the whole topic is Physics only. Particle motion in gases is in combined science too; it is pV = constant and work done on a gas that are Physics only.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer identifies which quantity is fixed before choosing a method, and says so. For a calculation it writes the constant on its own line, then divides, and checks that the pressure moved the way the physics requires. For an explanation it distinguishes the two cases precisely: heating changes both the frequency and the force of collisions, while compressing at constant temperature changes only the frequency, because the average speed depends on temperature alone. It recognises the word rapidly as a signal that work done on the gas raises its internal energy and temperature, so the constant-temperature condition no longer holds.
